newsitem.title: SPAIN: Analysts see perils in Spanish accounting moves.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see perils in Spanish accounting moves.

text.p: Spanish government efforts to wean bloated state companies off the public funds that have drip-fed them for years could leave it with a lurking debt burden, analysts said on Tuesday.
Spain last week announced it was sharply cutting subsidies to public sector companies in an effort to make them leaner.
Loss-making state companies will no longer be financed through the budget, but instead will use funds from profitable state-owned groups and the Treasury, Industry Minister Josep Pique said.

He estimated public sector firms would need 325 billion pesetas ($2.5 billion) in funds in 1997. Privatisation earnings or profits from profitable state-owned companies will provide 200 billion pestas and the Treasury the remaining 125 billion.

In addition, the state will guarantee up to 525 billion pesetas' worth of debt for public sector companies. Public sector companies currently clock up an estimated one trillion pesetas worth of debt every year.
The government is trying to spur efficiency among managers who have come to rely on government hand-outs during 13 years of Socialist rule.
"The government wants these firms to become responsible for their debts," according to an Economy Ministry spokeswoman.
But analysts said the new accounting measures create a grey area which could leave the government saddled with the debt of public companies in the next few years.

"There is always that risk when the state guarantees loans that it will eventually have to pay them," said one analyst in Madrid, pointing out that some public sector firms were incapable of making profits.
The government could sell off any resulting debt as part of a wide-ranging privatisation plan in 1997, said Craig Shute, analyst at Bear Stearns in London.
"If some of these firms are going to be sold in 1997, the deficit effectively turns over to private hands," he said.

But the most indebted companies will also be the most difficult to sell. For example, state railways company Renfe's poor management record and persistent losses make it almost impossible to privatise in the future, the Madrid analyst said.
The government may never have to account for any payment demands on loans it is guaranteeing for next year.

"You could postpone these debts forever," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "It's debatable and I think we will eventually need some rulings on this from the European Commission (EC)."

"It's not obvious where that (money) is going to be in (the budget in) 1998 or 1999," he added. "There is a bit of creative accounting going on across the board in Europe and Spain is one of the countries looking at these new methods."

In that respect, it was merely following the lead of other European countries in "fudging the books" to reduce the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, the level needed to join a single European currency, economists said.
France is relying on a one-off 37.5 billion franc ($7.4 billion) transfer from France Telecom to achieve its budget deficit target.

The issue has become political following comments by Italian Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco on Monday that some of Italy's European partners wanted to keep the country out of the first wave of European nations joining the economic and monetary union (EMU) due to begin in 1999.

"Spain and Italy are not particularly welcome in round one (of EMU)," said Lumholdt. "If France can fudge then Spain can fudge. This could constitute a problem if Spain is looking as good as France in early 1998." ($1= 128.3 Peseta)
